transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: Mr. Okonkwo, thank you for coming in to speak with me. I wanted to talk to you about your son's medication from yesterday.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I hope everything is alright. The other doctor told me that the dose was standard for his age and there was nothing to worry about.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: Well, I have to be honest, there was a mistake. We didn't actually weigh your son on the scale before we gave the medication. The dose was based on an estimate of his weight, and because of that, he received a dose that was significantly above the paediatric threshold.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Above the threshold? What does that even mean? You told me it was standard.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: It means the amount of drug was too high for his actual body weight. I am sorry for any confusion caused by the previous conversation, but we were really busy in the unit yesterday and some steps were missed.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I don't care how busy you were. This is my son. I am a leader in my community, I have people looking to me, and now I find out my child was given a dangerous amount of medicine because you didn't use a scale?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I can tell you're feeling very distressed and perhaps a bit betrayed right now.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Betrayed is a small word for it. My wife is terrified. If word gets out that I couldn't even ensure my own son's safety in this hospital—

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I understand, but let's look at the clinical side. We are monitoring his serum levels and his vitals are currently stable.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I am not talking about vitals, I am talking about my family's dignity and the safety of my boy. Why would anyone estimate a weight?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: It happens sometimes when things are moving quickly. Look, I actually have to go check on another patient in a few minutes, so I want to make sure we get through this.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: You have to go? I am telling you my life is being upended by a mistake here and you are checking your watch?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I'm just trying to be efficient. As I said, he is stable.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Stable is not the same as safe. What happens now? Who is taking responsibility for this?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: The team is handling it. We are keeping a close eye on him.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: That is not a plan. That is a sentiment.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: We will probably do some more blood tests later this week to make sure the drug has cleared his system.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Later this week? Which day? Which tests?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: Just general labs. We'll let you know if anything changes.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: You are not answering me. I need to know exactly what the risk is for his long-term health.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I'm sorry you're upset, but as I said, he's fine right now.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: You keep saying he is fine, but you started by saying he was given a dose above the safe limit. Those two things do not fit together.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: It just means it was higher than the recommended guideline. We're managing it.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I want to speak to the chief of medicine. I cannot trust the word of someone who estimates a child's weight.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I can see you're very angry. I'll see if I can get someone else to come by eventually.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Eventually? This is my son's life.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I really do have to get to my other patient now. I'll leave you with the nurse.

H.justification: Resident uses rushing language repeatedly ('I actually have to go', 'trying to be efficient', 'really do have to get to my other patient') and shows defensive escalation.

E.justification: The error is named explicitly, but the resident fails to check for comprehension and provides false reassurance by stating the child is 'fine' despite the overdose.

A.justification: The resident apologizes, but immediately dilutes it with an excuse ('we were really busy in the unit yesterday').

R.justification: While the resident names emotions ('distressed', 'betrayed', 'angry'), they consistently meet the patient's emotional bids with factual redirection to vitals and stability.

T.justification: The resident provides a vague step ('some more blood tests later this week') without a specific day, a named patient role, or a prevention plan.
